mainTopic: Brothers' rights after dividing an estate, the orphans' document and receipt, and the משנה on sharing the cost of a gatehouse and a city wall
overview: The amud opens with the sons of רב חסדא explaining that רב חמא followed the approach of נהרדעא. They show this from שמואל, who rules that brothers who divide an estate keep no path, window, ladder or water-channel rights over each other. רבא disagrees. רב חמא also rules that when a receipt is produced against an orphans' loan document, the court neither collects with it nor tears it up. רבינא follows רב חמא except in the receipt case, while מר זוטרא follows him there too. A new משנה then rules that neighbors can be forced to share the cost of a courtyard gatehouse and a city wall, and defines when a newcomer counts as a resident. The גמרא reconciles the gatehouse with a story about אליהו, giving four ways to tell a good gatehouse from one that blocks the poor. Next it explains the dispute with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and brings two versions of how רבי יוחנן said the wall cost is divided. Finally ריש לקיש and רבי יוחנן argue from פסוקים that Torah scholars need no wall, and that explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רב חמא follows the נהרדעא approach: brothers who divide keep no rights over each other
steps.stepSummary: The sons of רב חסדא explain that רב חמא's ruling follows the rabbis of נהרדעא. They bring שמואל's rule that brothers who split an estate have no path, window, ladder or water-channel rights over each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר ינוקא and מר קשישא, sons of רב חסדא, said to רב אשי: The rabbis of נהרדעא are following their usual reasoning. As רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: brothers who divided an inheritance have no right of way over each other, no window rights against each other, no ladder rights against each other, and no water-channel rights against each other. Be careful with these, because they are fixed laws.
steps.whatsHappening: Two scholars explain that רב חמא's ruling just before follows a known approach from his city, נהרדעא. They prove it from a ruling of שמואל, who was also from there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that רב חמא was following his city's tradition, not inventing a new idea. שמואל rules that once brothers divide, each portion is fully separate. The old arrangements from their father's time (paths, windows, ladders, water channels) do not carry over as rights against the other brother.

keyTerms.meaning: The rabbis of the city נהרדעא (שמואל's city)
Brothers who divided their father's estate

phrases.english: Mar Yenuka and Mar Kashisha,
sons of Rav Ḥisda, [said] to Rav Ashi:
The Sages of Neharde'a follow their own reasoning,
phrases.notes: He means רב חמא, who ruled just before. Like שמואל, he was from נהרדעא.

phrases.english: as Rav Naḥman said that Shmuel said:
Brothers who divided [their inheritance]

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לָהֶן לֹא דֶּרֶךְ זֶה עַל זֶה,
phrases.english: have no right of way against each other,
nor window rights against each other,
nor ladder rights against each other,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אַמַּת הַמַּיִם זֶה עַל זֶה,
phrases.english: nor water-channel rights against each other.
And be careful with these,
because they are established laws.

steps.triggerLanguage: נְהַרְדָּעֵי לְטַעְמַיְיהוּ – דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the source behind רב חמא's earlier ruling on the daf
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to שמואל, brothers who divided an estate have no path, window, ladder or water-channel rights over each other's portions.

steps.title: רבא disagrees: the brothers do keep these rights
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules the opposite of שמואל: brothers who divided do have these rights over each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: They do have them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא records that רבא disagrees with שמואל. In his view, the brothers keep all of these rights.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there are two opinions on brothers who divide. For שמואל (and so רב חמא), each brother may do as he wants on his own portion. For רבא, the path, window, ladder and water-channel rights still stay in place between them.

phrases.english: And Rava said: They do have [these rights].

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרָבָא אָמַר: יֵשׁ לָהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to שמואל's ruling
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבא, brothers who divided do keep path, window, ladder and water-channel rights over each other.
steps.whatToRemember: שמואל (followed by רב חמא) says divided brothers have no rights over each other's portions. רבא says they do.

steps.title: Orphans' loan document challenged by a receipt: no collecting, no tearing up
steps.stepSummary: Orphans held a loan document, and the borrower produced a receipt against it. רב חמא rules that we neither collect with the document nor tear it up, and explains both halves.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a loan document belonging to orphans, and a receipt came out against it. רב חמא said: We do not collect with it, and we do not tear it up. We do not collect with it, because a receipt came out against it. We do not tear it up, because when the orphans grow up, maybe they will bring proof and weaken the receipt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ruling of רב חמא, about a loan document the orphans inherited and a receipt saying the debt was already paid. He leaves the document on hold: no collecting, and no destroying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The receipt is enough to stop collection for now. But the orphans are young and cannot argue their case yet. When they grow up they might bring proof against the receipt, so the document is kept rather than torn up.

keyTerms.meaning: A loan document belonging to orphans
A receipt showing the debt was paid

phrases.english: There was a certain loan document of orphans,
against which a receipt came out.
phrases.notes: The borrower showed a receipt saying he had already paid this debt.

phrases.english: Rav Ḥama said:
We do not collect with it,
and we do not tear it up.
We do not collect with it
because a receipt came out against it.
We do not tear it up
because when the orphans grow up,
perhaps they will bring proof and undermine it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא שְׁטָרָא דְיַתְמֵי, דְּנָפֵיק עֲלֵיהּ תְּבָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since רב חמא's ruling was just discussed, the גמרא brings another ruling of his on a new topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a receipt is produced against orphans' loan document, the court neither collects with it nor tears it up, because the orphans may later prove the receipt false.
steps.confusionAlert: רב חמא is not saying the receipt is worthless. It does stop collection. He only refuses to destroy the document, in case the orphans later disprove the receipt.

steps.title: רב אחא בריה דרבא asks רבינא for the practical law
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרבא asks רבינא what the practical הלכה is.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא, son of רבא, said to רבינא: What is the הלכה?
steps.whatsHappening: After hearing these rulings, a student asks what the final practical law is. This sets up רבינא's decision in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question asks for a practical decision, not an explanation. It sets up a ruling covering the cases just discussed.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Aḥa, son of Rava, said to Ravina:
What is the halakha?

steps.triggerLanguage: הִלְכְתָא מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical ruling on the rulings just quoted
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the practical הלכה follows רב חמא's rulings

steps.title: רבינא: follow רב חמא, except in the receipt case
steps.stepSummary: רבינא rules that the הלכה follows רב חמא in all the cases except the receipt case. There we trust the receipt's witnesses and do not assume they lied.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: In all of them the הלכה follows רב חמא, except for the receipt, because we do not presume witnesses to be liars.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives the final ruling. Follow רב חמא everywhere, but in the orphans' case the receipt wins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חמא kept the document alive in case the receipt turned out false. רבינא rejects that worry, because the receipt is signed by witnesses and we assume witnesses tell the truth. So the receipt is trusted, and the loan document is not kept on hold.

keyTerms.meaning: In all of them (all these cases)
We do not presume them to be liars

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בְּכוּלְּהוּ הִלְכְתָא כְּרַב חָמָא,
phrases.english: He said to him: In all of them the halakha follows Rav Ḥama,
except for the receipt,
because we do not presume witnesses to be liars.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּכוּלְּהוּ הִלְכְתָא כְּרַב חָמָא, לְבַר מִתְּבָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The הלכה follows רב חמא in all cases except the receipt case, where the receipt is trusted.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Follow רב חמא in his rulings, but a receipt signed by witnesses is trusted against the orphans' loan document, since we do not assume witnesses lie.
steps.whatToRemember: רבינא's rule: follow רב חמא in all these cases except the receipt case. There the witnessed receipt is believed, because we do not assume witnesses are liars. The next step brings מר זוטרא, who disagrees about the receipt case.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a basic principle: a document signed by witnesses is presumed true. We do not hold off just because someone might later disprove it.

steps.title: מר זוטרא rules like רב חמא in the receipt case too
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא בריה דרב מרי disagrees with רבינא. He says the הלכה follows רב חמא in the receipt case as well, because a real receipt would have been shown while the father was alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא, son of רב מרי, said: In this case too, the הלכה follows רב חמא. If the receipt were real, the borrower should have shown it while the orphans' father was alive. Since he did not show it then, we can learn that he may have forged it.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא gives a different ruling from רבינא's ruling in Step 5. He says that even in the receipt case we follow רב חמא: we do not tear up the loan document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא said to trust the receipt. מר זוטרא says the timing makes the receipt suspicious. An honest borrower would have shown it to the lender himself, so showing it only to the orphans suggests it might be fake.

keyTerms.meaning: A receipt; a paper that 'breaks' (cancels) the loan document

steps.whatToRemember: On the receipt case there are two rulings. רבינא says we trust the receipt. מר זוטרא says we follow רב חמא, so we neither collect with the loan document nor tear it up.

phrases.aramaic: מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מָרִי אָמַר:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra, son of Rav Mari, said:
In this case too, the halacha follows Rav Chama;
phrases.notes: "This case" is the receipt case, the one case where רבינא had said not to follow רב חמא.

phrases.english: for if it were so that it is a valid receipt,
he should have produced it in their father's lifetime,
and since he did not produce it,
learn from this that he forged it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מָרִי אָמַר: בְּהָא נָמֵי הִלְכְתָא כְּרַב חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an opposing final ruling to רבינא's exception in Step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows רב חמא in the receipt case too, because a receipt shown only after the lender's death is suspect.

steps.title: משנה: Forcing Neighbors to Build a Gatehouse and Door
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that courtyard residents can force each other to help pay for a gatehouse and a door. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says not every courtyard needs a gatehouse.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: We force him to help build a gatehouse and a door for the courtyard. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: Not all courtyards need a gatehouse.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It says the neighbors in a shared courtyard can make each person chip in for a gatehouse and a door.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא gives a blanket rule: every courtyard can demand a gatehouse. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees and says it depends on the courtyard. One that does not really need a guard cannot force anyone to pay.

keyTerms.meaning: We force him (to pay his share)
A gatehouse, a small room at the entrance where a guard sits
A courtyard shared by several houses

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
We compel him to build
phrases.notes: "Him" means each person living in the courtyard. The others can force him to pay his share.

phrases.english: a gatehouse and a door for the courtyard.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא כׇּל הַחֲצֵרוֹת רְאוּיוֹת לְבֵית שַׁעַר.
phrases.english: Not all courtyards are fit for a gatehouse.

steps.triggerLanguage: כּוֹפִין אוֹתוֹ לִבְנוֹת בֵּית שַׁעַר וָדֶלֶת לֶחָצֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: the next משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Courtyard residents can force each other to fund a gatehouse and a door. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says only where the courtyard needs it.

steps.title: משנה: Forcing Townspeople to Build a City Wall
steps.stepSummary: The same rule applies to a city: residents can be forced to help pay for a wall, doors and a bar. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says not every town needs a wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: We force him to help build a wall, double doors and a bar for the city. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: Not all towns need a wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves from the courtyard to the whole city, giving the same kind of rule and the same disagreement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pattern repeats on a bigger scale. The city can force everyone to share the cost of protecting it. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל again says it depends on whether this town actually needs that protection.

keyTerms.meaning: A bar that locks the gates

phrases.english: We compel him to build for the city
a wall, double doors, and a bar.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Not all towns are fit for a wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: כּוֹפִין אוֹתוֹ לִבְנוֹת לָעִיר חוֹמָה וּדְלָתַיִם וּבְרִיחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the courtyard rule of Step 7 to a whole city.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: City residents can force each other to fund a wall, doors and a bar. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says only where the town needs a wall.

steps.title: משנה: When Someone Counts as a City Resident
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks how long a person must live in a city before he counts as a resident. It answers twelve months, or right away if he buys a house there.
steps.simpleTranslation: How long must a person be in the city to count like the people of the city? Twelve months. If he bought a house to live in there, he counts like the people of the city right away.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה defines who has to pay toward city projects like the wall. A newcomer becomes a resident after twelve months, or immediately if he buys a home.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This tells us exactly when a newcomer joins the duty to pay. Buying a home shows he plans to stay, so he becomes a resident at once without waiting a year.

keyTerms.meaning: Like the people of the city, a full resident

phrases.english: How long must he be in the city
and be like the people of the city?
Twelve months.
If he bought a residence in it,
he is like the people of the city immediately.

steps.triggerLanguage: כַּמָּה יְהֵא בָּעִיר וִיהֵא כְּאַנְשֵׁי הָעִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines who counts as a resident for the city duties of Step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person counts as a city resident after twelve months, or immediately if he buys a home there.

steps.title: Is a Gatehouse Really a Good Thing? The Story of אליהו
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה. A gatehouse seems to be a bad thing, because אליהו stopped talking to a חסיד after he built one.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Does this mean a gatehouse is a good thing? But there was a certain חסיד whom אליהו used to talk with regularly. He built a gatehouse, and אליהו did not talk with him anymore!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question on the משנה. If people can be forced to build a gatehouse, it must be good. Yet a story shows that building one cost a חסיד his visits from אליהו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה treats a gatehouse as something worth forcing people to pay for. The story suggests it is spiritually harmful. It is commonly explained that the guard keeps poor people from reaching the door to ask for צדקה.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this to say...? (opens a surprised question)

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Is this to say that a gatehouse is a good thing?!
But there was that pious man
with whom Eliyahu was accustomed
to talk with him;
he made a gatehouse,
and he did not talk with him anymore!

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דְּבֵית שַׁעַר מְעַלְּיוּתָא הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption in Step 7 that a gatehouse is beneficial.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's assumption that a gatehouse is good enough to force neighbors to fund.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: אליהו stopped visiting a חסיד because he built a gatehouse, which suggests a gatehouse is harmful.

steps.title: Inside Versus Outside Gatehouse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה means a gatehouse built inside the courtyard. The חסיד built his outside.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is on the inside, and that one is on the outside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the challenge by splitting the cases. The משנה is talking about a gatehouse built on the inside, while the חסיד's gatehouse was built on the outside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sources are true, but they describe different structures. A gatehouse inside the courtyard is good and can be required. One outside is the kind that drove away אליהו. As commonly explained, it fully blocks the poor from reaching the entrance.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction

steps.whatToRemember: First answer: the משנה's gatehouse is one built inside the courtyard, which is fine. The gatehouse that drove אליהו away was built outside. Steps 12-14 give other ways to split the cases.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is on the inside,
phrases.notes: "This" is the gatehouse in our משנה.

phrases.english: that is on the outside.
phrases.notes: "That" is the gatehouse the חסיד built in the story.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא מִגַּוַּאי, הָא מִבָּרַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 10 by telling apart two kinds of gatehouse.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All gatehouses are alike, so the משנה and the אליהו story contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה's gatehouse is inside the courtyard and is good. The חסיד's gatehouse was outside and was harmful.

steps.title: Second answer: a gatehouse with a door versus one without
steps.stepSummary: Both gatehouses can be outside. The difference is that one has a door that blocks the poor, and the other does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say both gatehouses were outside, and there is still no problem. One has a door, and the other has no door.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer to the same question from Step 10. This time it says both gatehouses were built outside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 said the difference was inside versus outside. Now the גמרא admits both could be outside and finds a new difference: a door. A door stops the poor from being heard, so that gatehouse is the bad one, like the gatehouse of the חסיד. A gatehouse with no door is the kind the משנה allows.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces another possible answer)
This one and that one, meaning both cases
And it is not a problem

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
this one and that one are outside,
phrases.notes: Both the gatehouse in the משנה and the gatehouse of the חסיד were outside the courtyard.

phrases.english: and it is not a problem:
this one has a door,
that one has no door.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא מִבָּרַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the question from Step 10. It replaces the inside/outside answer of Step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the cases by a new detail: whether the gatehouse has a door
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any gatehouse outside the courtyard would be bad, like the one the חסיד built
steps.terutzMaskana: Even an outside gatehouse is fine if it has no door, because the poor can still be heard

steps.title: Third answer: a door that needs a key versus one that does not
steps.stepSummary: Both gatehouses can have a door. The difference is that one door needs a key and the other does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say both have a door, and there is still no problem. One needs a key, and the other does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives yet another answer. It accepts that both gatehouses had doors and looks for a smaller difference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A door alone may not stop the poor if they can simply open it. A door that needs a key keeps them out, so that gatehouse is the bad kind. A door without a key is the kind the משנה allows.

keyTerms.meaning: A key, something used to open a lock

phrases.english: If you want, say:
this one and that one have a door,
and it is not a problem:
this one has a key,
that one has no key.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא דְּאִית לֵיהּ דֶּלֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on Step 12 by agreeing that both had doors, then finds a smaller difference.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the cases by whether a key is needed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any gatehouse with a door would block the poor
steps.terutzMaskana: A door that opens without a key is fine. Only a locked door is the problem.

steps.title: Fourth answer: the key kept inside versus outside
steps.stepSummary: Both doors can need a key. The difference is where the key is kept.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say both need a key, and there is still no problem. In one, the key is inside. In the other, the key is outside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its last answer. It agrees that both doors needed a key and asks where the key is kept.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the key is kept inside, the poor outside cannot reach it, so they are shut out. That is the bad case of the חסיד. If the key is kept outside, they can reach it, so the gatehouse does not block them. Each of these answers says the same thing: a gatehouse is only bad when it keeps the poor away.
steps.whatToRemember: All four answers (Steps 11 to 14) agree on one idea. The משנה allows a gatehouse that does not keep poor people away. The חסיד was punished for a gatehouse that did keep them away.

phrases.english: If you want, say:
this one and that one have a key,
and it is not a problem:
this one, where its key is inside,
that one, where its key is outside.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא דְּאִית לֵיהּ פּוֹתַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on Step 13 by agreeing that both needed a key, then finds a smaller difference.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the cases by where the key is kept
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any door that needs a key would block the poor
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a key kept inside, out of the reach of the poor, makes the gatehouse bad

steps.title: Which courtyards need a gatehouse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה and brings a ברייתא. In it, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says only a courtyard next to the public area needs a gatehouse.
steps.simpleTranslation: We force him to help build a gatehouse and a door for the courtyard. A ברייתא teaches that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says not every courtyard needs a gatehouse. A courtyard next to the public area needs one. A courtyard not next to the public area does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the words of the משנה. It brings a ברייתא that explains what רבן שמעון בן גמליאל meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only said that not every courtyard needs a gatehouse. The ברייתא gives the exact rule: it depends on whether the courtyard is next to the public area, where people pass by and can look in.

keyTerms.meaning: We force (each resident to pay his share)
A gatehouse, a small room at the entrance
The public area, such as a street

phrases.english: We force him to build
a gatehouse and a door for the courtyard.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא כָּל חֲצֵרוֹת רְאוּיוֹת לְבֵית שַׁעַר;
phrases.english: not all courtyards are fit for a gatehouse;
rather, a courtyard that is next to the public area
is fit for a gatehouse,
and one that is not next to the public area
is not fit for a gatehouse.

steps.triggerLanguage: כּוֹפִין אוֹתוֹ לִבְנוֹת בֵּית שַׁעַר וָדֶלֶת לֶחָצֵר. תַּנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story of the חסיד and goes back to explain the משנה from Step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, only a courtyard next to the public area needs a gatehouse.

steps.title: Why the רבנן say every courtyard needs a gatehouse
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן say every courtyard needs a gatehouse, because crowds in the street sometimes push people into any courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן? Sometimes people in the public area get pushed, and they come in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks, without saying it out loud, why the רבנן disagree with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. Then it answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן agree that the point of a gatehouse is to keep the public out. But they say that even a courtyard far from the street can get people pushed into it when the street is crowded. So every courtyard needs one.

keyTerms.meaning: And the רבנן? (a short way of asking why they disagree)
That they are pushed or crowded

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not written out. The single word וְרַבָּנַן means: and why don't the רבנן agree? The rest of the line is the answer.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis?
phrases.notes: This one word is the question: why don't they make the same split as רבן שמעון בן גמליאל?

phrases.english: sometimes the people of the public area are pushed,
and they enter and come in.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן – זִימְנִין דְּדָחֲקִי בְּנֵי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the other side of the argument in Step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Crowds can push people into any courtyard, so every courtyard needs a gatehouse.

steps.title: Which cities need a wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה and brings a ברייתא. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says only a city near the border needs a wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: We force him to build for the city, and so on. The רבנן taught: we force him to make doors and a bar for the city. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says not every city needs a wall. A city near the border needs one. A city not near the border does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the next line of the משנה, about the city. It brings a ברייתא that works the same way as the one about the courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This copies the courtyard case. A wall protects a city from enemies, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that danger is real only for a city near the border.

keyTerms.meaning: Double doors and a bar that locks them

phrases.english: We force him to build for the city, and so on.
phrases.notes: Another quote from the משנה. The "and so on" stands for the wall, doors and bar from Step 8.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: כּוֹפִין אוֹתוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת לָעִיר דְּלָתַיִם וּבְרִיחַ.
phrases.english: We force him to make double doors and a bar for the city.
And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
not all cities are fit for a wall;
rather, a city that is next to the border
is fit for a wall,
and one that is not next to the border
is not fit for a wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: כּוֹפִין אוֹתוֹ לִבְנוֹת לָעִיר כּוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Does for the city in Step 8 what Step 15 did for the courtyard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, only a city near the border needs a wall.

steps.title: Why the רבנן say every city needs a wall
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן say every city needs a wall, because an enemy army can sometimes reach any area.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן? Sometimes it happens that an army comes.
steps.whatsHappening: Once again the גמרא asks, without saying it out loud, why the רבנן disagree. It answers that troops can show up anywhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being far from the border lowers the danger but does not remove it. Since an army can sometimes march deep into the country, the רבנן say every city should be protected.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis?
sometimes it happens that an army comes.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן – זִימְנִין דְּמִקְּרוּ וְאָתֵי גְּיָיסָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the other side of the argument in Step 17, the same way Step 16 did for the courtyard.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An army can reach any city, so every city needs a wall.

steps.title: How is the cost of the wall divided?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר asks רבי יוחנן whether the money is collected by the number of people or by how much money each person has.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר asked רבי יוחנן: when they collect, do they collect by the number of people, or by wealth?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. The residents have to pay for the wall, but how much does each person pay?
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two fair-sounding choices. Each person could pay the same share, since everyone's life is protected. Or the rich could pay more, since a wall protects property and they have more to lose.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar asked Rabbi Yochanan:
when they collect,
phrases.notes: He means collecting money from the residents to build the city wall.

phrases.english: do they collect according to the number of people,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִילְמָא לְפִי שֶׁבַח מָמוֹן גּוֹבִין?
phrases.english: or maybe they collect according to the amount of wealth?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from whether a wall is needed to how its cost is divided.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the cost of the wall divided by the number of people or by wealth?

steps.title: The cost is divided by wealth, and this is firm
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that the money is collected by wealth. He tells רבי אלעזר to hold on to this ruling firmly.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: they collect by wealth. And Elazar my son, fix nails in it!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question. He adds strong words to show that this ruling must not be changed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person with more property has more to lose and gains more from the wall, so he pays more. The phrase about fixing nails means this ruling is fastened in place like something nailed down.

keyTerms.meaning: Fix nails in it, meaning hold this ruling firm

steps.whatToRemember: In this first version, the cost of a city wall is shared by wealth, not by the number of people, and רבי יוחנן says this הלכה is fixed. The next step brings a second version (איכא דאמרי) with a different answer.
steps.whyThisMatters: This version ties the wall cost to property, since a wall protects property. The second version in steps 21-22 ties it to how close each house is to the wall.

phrases.english: He said to him:
they collect according to wealth;
and Elazar, my son,
fix nails in it!
phrases.notes: In plain words: this ruling is settled, so hold on to it and don't move from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לְפִי מָמוֹן גּוֹבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of רבי אלעזר in Step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The money is collected by wealth, and this is a firm הלכה.

steps.title: Second version: what is the basis for collecting wall money?
steps.stepSummary: Some report that רבי אלעזר asked רבי יוחנן a different version of the question: is wall money collected by how close the houses are to the wall, or by wealth?
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say the question went like this: רבי אלעזר asked רבי יוחנן, when they collect money for the wall, do they collect by how close the houses are, or perhaps by how much money people have?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another version of the same conversation from steps 19-20, with different options in the question. This sets up a different answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the choice was 'by number of people' or 'by wealth.' Here the choice is 'by how close the house is to the wall' or 'by wealth.' The idea behind closeness is that houses near the wall are more exposed, so they gain more from it.

keyTerms.meaning: How close the houses are (to the wall)

phrases.english: Some say:

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar asked Rabbi Yochanan:
When they collect,
do they collect according to how close the houses are,
phrases.notes: He means how close each house is to the wall.

phrases.english: or perhaps they collect according to wealth?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of the question asked in step 19.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the wall tax divided by how close each house is to the wall, or by each person's wealth?

steps.title: Collect by how close the houses are
steps.stepSummary: In this version, רבי יוחנן answers that the money is collected by how close the houses are to the wall, and tells רבי אלעזר to hold on to this firmly.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: they collect by how close the houses are. And Elazar my son, fix nails in this ruling!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question: whoever lives closer to the wall pays more. He tells his student to treat this ruling as firmly fixed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version (step 20) the answer was wealth. In this version it is closeness of the houses. The same strong phrase, 'fix nails in it', shows up in both versions, so each version claims to be the firm ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: Fix nails in it: hold this ruling firmly

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two versions. In the first one (step 20) the answer is 'by wealth.' In this one it is 'by closeness of the houses.'

phrases.english: He said to him:
They collect according to how close the houses are;
and Elazar my son, fix nails in it!
phrases.notes: Like nailing something down, he means: this ruling is firm, don't budge from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לְפִי קֵירוּב בָּתִּים הֵן גּוֹבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The wall tax is collected by how close each house is to the wall.

steps.title: Do Torah scholars have to pay for the wall?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה נשיאה charged the חכמים for the wall. ריש לקיש objected that Torah scholars don't need protection, and brought a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה נשיאה put the wall tax on the חכמים. ריש לקיש said: the חכמים don't need protection, as it is written, 'If I count them, they are more than sand.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new story starts: the leader charged the Torah scholars for the city wall. ריש לקיש says they shouldn't pay, and quotes a פסוק that the גמרא will now explain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wall is for protection, so someone who doesn't need protection shouldn't have to pay for it. ריש לקיש claims Torah scholars are already protected, but the פסוק he brings doesn't clearly say that yet. The next steps will show how he reads it.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי יהודה the Nasi (leader), a grandson of רבי יהודה הנשיא

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
imposed the wall tax on the Sages.
Reish Lakish said:
The Sages do not need protection,
as it is written: "If I count them, they are more than the sand"

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה נְשִׂיאָה רְמָא דְּשׁוּרָא אַדְּרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: whether Torah scholars are exempt from the wall tax.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ריש לקיש: Torah scholars do not need protection, so they should not pay for the wall.

steps.title: Who are the ones 'more than sand'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks who the פסוק is counting. It can't mean the צדיקים themselves, because all of Israel together is only 'like the sand.'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If I count them': who? If you say the צדיקים are more than the sand, that's a problem. All of Israel is described as 'like the sand on the seashore.' Could the צדיקים alone be more than the sand?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the simple reading of the פסוק. If all of Israel is only as many as the sand, a smaller group, the צדיקים, can't be more than the sand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The צדיקים are just one part of Israel. A part can't be bigger than the whole, so the פסוק must be counting something other than the people themselves.

keyTerms.meaning: Whom? To whom does it refer?
If you say: introduces a suggested answer that will be rejected
Now (if this is true): introduces a 'how could that be' argument

phrases.english: "If I count them": whom?
If you say it means the righteous,
that they are more numerous than the sand,
now, about all of Israel it is written:
"like the sand on the seashore,"
could the righteous themselves be "more than the sand"?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶסְפְּרֵם לְמַאן? אִילֵימָא לְצַדִּיקִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the plain reading of the פסוק ריש לקיש quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading the פסוק as saying the צדיקים themselves are more than the sand.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: All of Israel is only 'like the sand,' so a smaller part of Israel can't be 'more than the sand.'

steps.title: It is the deeds of the צדיקים that outnumber the sand
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the פסוק is counting the good deeds of the צדיקים, and those are more than the sand.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what it means: if I count the deeds of the צדיקים, they are more than the sand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge: the פסוק isn't counting the people, it's counting their good deeds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the counting is about deeds and not people, the problem from step 24 is gone. A small group can easily have more good deeds than there are grains of sand. This reading sets up the proof in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, this is what it is saying

phrases.english: Rather, this is what it is saying:
If I count the deeds of the righteous,
they are more than the sand.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָכִי קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24 by reading the פסוק differently.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the פסוק: it counts deeds, not people.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק counts the צדיקים themselves.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק counts the deeds of the צדיקים, which are more than the sand.

steps.title: A קל וחומר: if sand protects, good deeds surely protect
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש's reading ends with a קל וחומר: sand, which is fewer, holds back the sea, so the many deeds of the צדיקים surely protect them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is a קל וחומר: sand, which is less, protects against the sea. The deeds of the צדיקים, which are more, surely protect the צדיקים!
steps.whatsHappening: Now the proof is finished. Sand holds back the sea, and the deeds of the צדיקים are even more than sand, so those deeds surely protect them. That's why the חכמים don't need a wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק itself only says the deeds are more than sand. The קל וחומר adds the point that matters here: sand protects, so something greater than sand protects even more. This ties the פסוק back to ריש לקיש's claim that the חכמים are exempt from paying for the wall.

keyTerms.meaning: An 'all the more so' argument, from a lighter case to a stronger one

steps.whatToRemember: ריש לקיש: the good deeds of Torah scholars protect them more than sand holds back the sea, so they don't need to pay for a city wall.

phrases.english: And it follows all the more so:
If sand, which is fewer,
protects against the sea,
the deeds of the righteous, which are many,
surely all the more so they protect them!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְקַל וָחוֹמֶר: וּמָה חוֹל, שֶׁמּוּעָט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the new reading in step 25 to prove ריש לקיש's claim.
steps.raayaObject: Torah scholars are protected and don't need the wall.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A קל וחומר from sand holding back the sea, based on תהלים 139:18.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן suggests a better פסוק: 'I am a wall'
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש tells רבי יוחנן what happened. רבי יוחנן asks why he didn't quote 'I am a wall and my breasts are like towers' and starts explaining it: the wall is the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: When ריש לקיש came before רבי יוחנן, רבי יוחנן said to him: why didn't you tell him from this פסוק: 'I am a wall and my breasts are like towers'? 'I am a wall': this is the תורה. 'And my breasts are like towers':
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן offers a different פסוק that proves the same point more directly. He begins explaining it, and the explanation continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש needed a long reading plus a קל וחומר to reach his point. רבי יוחנן's פסוק mentions a 'wall' outright and explains that the wall is the תורה, so תורה itself is the protection. The second half of the explanation, about the 'towers', comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.term: מַאי טַעְמָא לָא תֵּימָא לֵיהּ מֵהָא
keyTerms.meaning: Why didn't you tell him from this (source)?

phrases.english: When he came before Rabbi Yochanan,
phrases.notes: 'He' is ריש לקיש, coming to tell his teacher what happened.

phrases.english: he said to him:

phrases.aramaic: מַאי טַעְמָא לָא תֵּימָא לֵיהּ מֵהָא:
phrases.english: Why didn't you tell him from this:
"I am a wall and my breasts are like towers";
"I am a wall": this is the Torah,
"and my breasts are like towers":

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא לָא תֵּימָא לֵיהּ מֵהָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different, more direct פסוק for the same claim ריש לקיש proved in steps 23-26.
steps.raayaObject: Torah scholars are protected by the תורה and don't need the wall.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שיר השירים 8:10, 'I am a wall', read as referring to the תורה.
